**How to measure this codebase without lying to yourself.**

Read this **before writing a probe, making a count, or claiming that something does not
exist**. It is not needed for ordinary editing, which is why it lives here instead of in
`CLAUDE.md` — it was one 12,000-character bullet there, paid for on every turn of every
session, and unreadable as a single line.

Every rule below was earned by an instrument that **failed while looking like it worked**.
The examples are kept because they are the evidence; strip them and this becomes advice.

---

## 0. The one-question diagnostic

This is the durable part. Everything else is elaboration.

> **If this control came out the other way, would the CLAIM be false, or would the
> INSTRUMENT be broken?**

- **Claim control** — bears on whether the claim is true. **Must test the same symbol.**
- **Instrument control** — evidence the detector can *see*. Its defining property is a
  **known expected answer**, not a different symbol.
- **A control answering neither is vacuous.** A claim about `kLootChestTables` was
  "refuted" by a sweep of `BlockId` — 16 hits, 0 in asserts, **every digit true and
  bearing on nothing.** That is more convincing than a wrong number, precisely because it
  survives checking.

⚠️ **Ship the diagnostic with its known blind spot: it cannot see a wrong-token claim**,
where the honest answer is *neither* — the claim is false and the instrument is flawless.

---

## 1. What a control must be

A control must **differ from the claim in exactly one variable**, and then **fire**,
**differ in direction**, **differ by a plausible magnitude**, and **not be vacuous on both
sides**. "The control fired" is not the test.

**The one-variable rule is the capstone, because every failure is two variables moving or
none.** A probe's `$LF` constant and `$lf` counter are **the same variable in PowerShell**,
so claim and control were computed from one corrupted value, and the control returned
exactly what was expected while testing nothing.

Then: one broken detector returned `1` for its claim *and* `1` for its control. Another
returned 0/0 across thirteen files — **agreement of two zeros is not agreement.**

- **A graded control settles all five** — plant one fault and see 1, plant three and see 3.
  Prefer a graded control of **real strings with known counts** (1, 1, 0) over a single
  invented token.
- **A control must exercise the same character classes as the claim.** `[regex]::Escape($s)`
  together with `-SimpleMatch` is a **double escape** — the escape turns a space into `\ `,
  then `-SimpleMatch` hunts that backslash literally. Five probes verifying text that had
  just been written correctly all returned **0**, and the invented-name control returned its
  expected 0 **because it contained no space**, leaving the escape a no-op on it alone.
  **The instrument was blind exactly where the claim lived, and the control was blind to the
  blindness** — one step from reverting a correct edit.
- **Give a control the same SHAPE as its subject:** same spaces, same punctuation, the same
  trip through whatever escaping the probe applies.
- **The strongest control is drawn from the KNOWN-FAILURE SET, not designed.** You cannot
  know in advance which region your instrument is weak in, so a control you invented
  yourself has no power over it. Use the exact tokens a prior instrument got wrong.

**Tells that the instrument, not the world, produced your number:**

- **Uniformity.** A suspicious cluster of identical values has exposed a broken instrument
  twice — though once it was real (four consecutive `case` labels), so it is a prompt to
  check the tool, not proof it is broken.
- **Impossibility.** If literal rows > declared array size, **your counter is broken** — the
  compiler would have rejected the file. A count of 12 literals in a 6-element array is
  nested braces being double-counted. **Report no result rather than a number.**
- **An empty declared-set** for an enum you know exists means a broken extractor. Report no
  result rather than a hundred false errors.

---

## 2. Absence claims — the four legs

**"X does not exist", "nothing calls this", "no caller".** This is the claim type this
project gets wrong most often. **Measured: wrong five times in eight, then six in six, then
seven more — and never once in the other direction.** `"X is missing"` is the least reliable
sentence in this repository; `"X is broken"` is far sounder.

**An absence claim can never have a claim control** — its whole content is that there is
nothing to measure. That is why it needs the other three.

### ⓪ Is this token the only way the concept could be spelled?

**No control can answer this.** It is the leg that kills claims.

A claim that `BeeNest` was unplaced came with two flawless controls — 45 hits in-file, 39
for the same symbol elsewhere, non-uniform, invented name 0 — **and was still false, because
`beeNest` case-insensitively returns 11 in that very file**, the id being built by
`beeNestAtLevel`.

**Five wrong claims died here in one night:** that one, `ChainmailHelmet + piece`, sixteen
`CreatureKind` written by **index cast**, seventeen `BiomeId` by `static_cast`, and
`familyRoughness` reaching the GPU **through a packed row**.

**⚠️ Prefixes are part of ⓪, and this codebase is built out of id runs.** `Enum::Name` is a
prefix of `Enum::NameFirst` and `Enum::NameLast`. `BlockId::Vine` measured **8 unanchored
and 4 word-bounded — and does not exist**, while four `static_assert`s used it. **Word-bound
every enum probe, and say which enum you measured** — `Vine` is declared in `BlockShape`,
and `BlockShape ∩ BlockId = ∅`.

**⚠️ A field name can belong to two structs.** `CreatureSpecies::halfWidth` measures 72 hits;
`ProjectileSpecies::halfWidth` measures 6. An unscoped `\bhalfWidth\b` returns ~78 and
**buries a true zero-readers claim under another type's traffic.** A bare identifier count is
meaningless until you have named which type owns it.

**⓪ has an audit-level form: is this SET the only way the blocker could be counted?** One
count listed enumerators when the population that mattered was recipes — **and a recipe is
blocked by its inputs as well as its output**, so counting outputs alone undercounts.
**Listing beats counting only when you list the right population; otherwise it is a more
confident count.**

**For a table there is a mechanical answer to ⓪ that needs no guess about how a hidden row
might be spelled:** compare the array's **declared size** against the **count of literal
enumerators in its initialiser**. A row produced by a cast, by arithmetic or in a loop adds
to the declared size but not the literal count, so any non-literal spelling shows as a
shortfall. `27 declared == 27 literal` proves a token search *could not* have been fooled.

### ① A same-symbol, different-file probe

In a file where the token is **known** to appear. **For an absence claim this is the
strongest evidence available, because it alone proves the detector sees that exact token** —
a different symbol at 45 hits fires cheerfully while a broken pattern for the real name
returns 0.

**⚠️ The positive control must come from the same SYNTACTIC NEIGHBOURHOOD as the target.**
An enumerator extractor lacking multiline dropped every enumerator preceded by a doc comment
and then reported absence about everything — and its three positive controls passed **only
because all three happened to be undocumented enumerators.**

**And the first version of that correction was itself wrong.** "Use a *documented*
enumerator" is necessary but not sufficient: `ItemId::TurtleHelmet` is documented and it
passed. **The discriminator is doc-block LENGTH, not presence** — a look-back-one-line
extractor handles a 1-line block and fails on a 3–4 line one. In `ItemId` only 2 of 26
documented enumerators are 1-line, so a randomly drawn control catches the bug ~92% of the
time, and the failing draw is the one that ships a false STOP.

**⚠️ Four enums here are declared on a SINGLE LINE** — `ArmourSlot`, `FluidKind`,
`Placement`, `DragButton` — **and a per-line extractor drops 8 of their 12 enumerators.**
**Require two structurally different extractors to agree before believing any absence.**

### ② A different-symbol, same-file probe

Including a name **invented on the spot** that must return 0, so that a zero on the subject
carries information.

### ③ The probe count, computed from the results and never narrated

The agent that gave us this rule printed `Probes landed: 3 of 4` as a **hardcoded string
inside its own demonstration of the rule**, when the real value was 2 of 4. **A narrated
count is indistinguishable from a real one.**

### ④ For a behavioural absence, follow the data, not just the name

An instrument control proves the detector works; only tracing the gate proves the behaviour
cannot occur. `inFire = inFire || block == BlockId::Fire` is **one equality against one
enumerator**, so no campfire id can satisfy that flag — structural, and materially stronger
than any name count.

**⚠️ Trace it to the END, because the same follow says what else exists.** Campfires *do*
burn you, via a separate `inCampfire` beside it — so the correct reading was never "campfire
damage is absent" but "it cannot come through *this* flag". **A data-follow that stops at the
gate it set out to check will report an absence that is really a redirection.**

## 3. How the value ARRIVES, before you count anything about its name

**Only a field answers to a writer-count. Only a free function answers to a call-site
count.** Everything else — parameter, struct member, table row, cast — needs the caller
traced.

**A writer-count on a PARAMETER is structurally always zero**, because the caller fills it,
at the call site, under its own name. `wearingLeather` measured **0 writers and 3 readers —
every digit true and the conclusion false** — while the state lived in two `PlayerInput`
fields filled in `Main.cpp` and OR'd into the argument at the call site.

**⚠️ And that only tells you where to look NEXT, not the answer. The two directions fail
oppositely:**

- counting a parameter's writers says **dead-when-live**
- checking only the call site says **live-when-dead** — ask "who calls this and what do they
  pass" and these same flags answer *"an argument is supplied, looks live"* while both were
  still dead.

**Walk to the field, then ask who writes the field.** The real chain was five hops:
`Main.cpp` writes → a `PlayerInput` field → an OR at the call site → the parameter → the
reader.

**This reached eleven agents as a CRITICAL** saying leather gave no powder-snow immunity, and
obeying it meant **adding a second writer to a value with exactly one owner** — bug shape #1
— against an instruction in `Player.hpp` reading verbatim *"Do not add a second filling
site."*

> **The wording was half the defect.** It began as a cross-file handoff request and was
> actioned within sixteen minutes, so *"nothing writes these"* turned into a false defect
> report **at the moment it succeeded**. Write *"these need filling, as of 11:11"* instead —
> **a handoff phrased as a permanent negative rots into a bug report the instant someone does
> the work.**

---

## 4. A measurement is a fact with a timestamp

**Record "already fixed", never "never broken".**

An agent measured `Block.hpp`, found `BlockId::Vine` absent, and concluded the reported bug
had never existed — asking to halt the fleet. **Committed HEAD settled it: 4 word-bounded
uses in the committed file, fixed 12 minutes before it looked.**

Another agent hit the identical setup and did not take the bait, because
`BlockId::VineFirst` went **0→4 in the same file**: *a fix leaves positive evidence, not just
an absence.*

- **When your measurement contradicts a report, check the file's mtime against the report's
  timestamp BEFORE concluding the report was wrong.** `git show HEAD:<path>` settles it
  outright and is read-only.
- **The opposite direction is commoner:** a claim of absence going stale as things get built.
  Six documents carried one in a single session. **Date every negative claim and name its
  falsifier** — one written at 13:35 was falsified at 13:41.
- **A prior "not yet built" note is the most dangerous kind, because it is often phrased as
  an IMPERATIVE and no negative-word search can reach it.** `Copper.hpp` carried a precise
  work order for eight table rows **that were already done**; honouring it would have added
  40 ids and **renumbered every saved world**. Sweep for instruction-shaped comments —
  *"write"*, *"add"*, *"the fix is"*, *"needs a"*, *"should call"* — and for each, ask
  whether it has already been done.

## 5. Probe mechanics that lie

| Trap | What happens |
|---|---|
| **A failed regex anchor returns the WHOLE FILE, not zero** | A failed `Match` leaves `Index = 0`, so a brace-matcher spans the entire file. One probe reported a **673,449-character "span"** and a plausible count. **Print whether your anchor bound anything.** |
| **`-Include` without `-Recurse` returns ZERO files** | It filters the path. **Print the CORPUS size** — a count of the subject can look plausible; a count of the corpus cannot lie quietly. |
| **`$hash.Count` returns the KEY NAMED `Count`** | And `Count` is an enumerator in most of these id families. Use `$hash.Keys.Count` and `ContainsKey()`. |
| **`Select-String` is case-INSENSITIVE; the `grep` tool is case-SENSITIVE** | The same pattern gave "no matches" vs 4. And `kEye` matched **"keyed"** in prose — 6 where the truth was 3. `\b` on the right cannot help; the collision is on the left. **Use `-CaseSensitive` for any camelCase or `k`-prefixed identifier.** |
| **PowerShell `-Filter` has no character classes** | `-Filter 'water[0-9]*.png'` reported 0 when all 32 files existed. |
| **A build verdict must rest on an EXIT CODE, never a text pattern** | `error C` misses `Command line error D8036`; empty output satisfies every pattern; and `%ERRORLEVEL%` in a single-line `&`-chained `cmd` **expands at parse time and prints 0 on a failed build**. |
| **`check-ascii.ps1` reports green on files that do not exist** | A multi-path invocation joins the paths. **Read the reported line, not the exit code** — the tell is a byte count of 0. |
| **`.ninja_deps` answered 1 for six of seven headers** | Its paths are interned by index. |
| **A probe that finds no table has not found an absent table** | A `kBiomes` sweep of `Biome.hpp` returned nothing because the table lives in `Biome.cpp`. **Say which file you actually opened**, or the silence reads as a clean bill. |
| **A wrong-scope probe manufactures exactly the alarm you are hunting** | `itemForBlock` was reported undeclared because the probe only opened `Block.hpp`; it is declared in `Item.hpp`. **Every "does not exist" needs its search scope stated alongside it.** |

**Anchor a table regex on the REAL declaration.** One probe required `kTools\s*=\s*\{`; the
array is brace-initialised `std::array<ToolRule, 27> kTools{{` **with no `=` at all**, so the
pattern mis-anchored 850 bytes downfield and reported a 35-byte table with **zero pickaxes
and zero swords** — caught only by two positive controls.

**Prose search in C++ is biased toward FALSE ABSENCE.** A phrase search returned 0 while
three phrases from the same comment returned 1 — **the sentence wraps, and no contiguous
search crosses a newline plus a `// ` prefix.** Normalise (strip `//`, collapse whitespace)
or use `git diff`, never the phrase.

**A whole-file regex counts comments, and this codebase writes falsifiers INTO comments.**
`BlockId::Waxed` was flagged undeclared twice — both hits inside `///` blocks telling a
reader to search for exactly that token. **Flag every hit CODE or COMMENT.** A
`static_assert` count that swallowed one quoted inside a doc block gave six where there are
five, and that off-by-one shifted every index so the **wrong count and the wrong verdict had
one cause, each making the other look confirmed**.

**A comment that records what it REPLACED will always trip a sweep for the phrase it
replaced.** After correcting two stale claims, a sweep for the old wording still returned 1
each — both the agent's own quotations, refuted in the next clause. **List the hits and read
them.**

> **The root cause under every broken detector: punctuation and column position are proxies
> for grammar, and a proxy fails exactly where the grammar reuses the punctuation.** `(` and
> `,` delimit parameter lists *and* template argument lists; column zero starts definitions
> *and* signatures. That is one sentence for the `kTools` mis-anchor, the
> `std::array<…,\d+>` blindness to derived sizes, the doc-comment `static_assert` miscount,
> and a close-out check's false-presence failure.

## 6. Tables, and the bug the compiler will not report

**`std::array` silently ZERO-FILLS a short initialiser.** Too *long* is a hard error; too
*short* is not. A `kFlowers` declared 12 with 11 rows quietly places `BlockId` 0 — **Air, as
a flower** — on a clean build with no warning.

**The detector is declared size vs literal row count**, and it is the same check as ⓪'s
mechanical form. **Run it even where the size is DERIVED** — derivation fixes
*declared-vs-enum* but **not** *literal-vs-declared*.

**A table is only protected if its all-defaults row is INVALID.** `kTables` escapes because
`poolCount == 0` is independently rejected. `kEntries` does not, because the NSDMI weight `1`
is also the commonest real weight — so a lost row passes **all four** of its asserts and an
emerald becomes a weighted-nothing forever. **Derive the check from intent** (count the
deliberate empty rows and assert the count), not from the size.

**Choose the literal token per table rather than reusing one generic pattern.** That is what
makes a run of them worth believing: `kOreVeins` 9/9, `kSurfaceAtOrAbove` 25/25, `kFlowers`
12/12, `kCorals` 5/5, `kStalls` 4/4.

---

## 7. Reporting

- **When the candidate set is small, stop counting and LIST it**, flagging each hit as code
  or comment.
- **A finding that says STOP is held to a higher bar than one that says FIX, and must carry
  its own control** — because a stop is **self-sealing**: nobody who obeys it will ever
  generate the evidence that refutes it. An undeclared-symbol claim is always a STOP.
- **When you must choose a direction to fail in, choose FALSE ALARM.** A false all-clear goes
  quiet; a false alarm gets checked.
- **Controls verify the INSTRUMENT; they cannot verify the POPULATION.** A claim of "20
  pieces, not 24" was wrong at 25/25 because the sixth material is `Emberite`, a coined name
  no reference-derived list could contain. Every control passed throughout.
- **A rule derived from one instance is the same defect as a claim derived from one grep.**
  The three corrections this standard needed in one evening — *same symbol*, then *different
  symbol*, then *print the count* — were each generalised from a single case and each
  falsified by a case nobody went looking for.

## Where this came from

Extracted from `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-08-19, where it had grown into a single
12,199-character bullet — 20% of a file attached to every session, and paid for on every
turn whether or not anyone was measuring anything. Nothing was dropped in the move; the
2026-08-19 additions (the prefix trap, corpus size, the neighbourhood control, single-line
enums, the timestamp rule) are new.

**Companions:** `CLAUDE.md` holds the hard rules and the bug shapes; `LESSONS.md` holds every
mistake already paid for, including the fourteen instrument failures of 2026-08-19.
